utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-84bis-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al., Idriz Balaj, Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Let me take the opportunity to welcome everybody. Mr. Haradinaj, Mr. Balaj, and Mr. Brahimaj, particularly to all three of you. Can all of you hear me in a language you understand? Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we please have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Paul Rogers appearing on behalf of the Prosecutor, together today with Ms. Daniela Kravetz, Ms. Barbara Goy, and our Case Manager, Ms. Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ben Emmerson on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj, together with Rodney Dixon and Annie O'Reilly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Idriz Balaj, along with Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, and our intern, Alexander Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Richard Harvey for Mr. Brahimaj, accompanied by Ms. Sophie Rigney. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey. Now, the next item I would like us to deal with is the purpose of the hearing. As we all know, the last Status Conference in this case was held on the 23rd of February, 2011. The Trial Chamber is required, pursuant to Rule 65 bis, to hold a Status Conference within 120 days after the last Status Conference, A, to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure expeditious preparation for trial; B, to review the status of the accused's case and to allow the accused to raise issues in relation thereto; C, to allow the accused to raise issues in relation his mental and physical condition and matters relating detention. A meeting of the chairmanship of the SLO and pursuant to Rule 65 ter was convened yesterday to prepare for this Status Conference. Am I right that far? That's correct. On the 31st of May, 2011, the Appeals Chamber issued two decisions dismissing the interlocutory appeals filed by Haradinaj, Balaj, and Brahimaj against the Trial Chamber decision on the shortened form of the fourth amended indictment of the 14th of January, 2011. In accordance with the Appeals Chamber decisions, the operative indictment in this case is the indictment filed by the Prosecutor on the 21st of January, 2011, in compliance with the Trial Chamber decision of 14 January 2011. With this matter now resolved, the Chamber is able to move ahead with the final preparations for the start of the re-trial. And if I may address myself to the Prosecution on the next point, which I know is not the business of the pre-trial phase, it's the business of the Trial Chamber really. It's not the business of the Pre-Trial Judge. However, in preparation for the Pre-Trial Conference I just wanted to say to you, Mr. Rogers, pursuant to Rule 73 bis of the Rules, the Trial Chamber may call upon the Prosecution to shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief for some witnesses or may invite the Prosecution to reduce the number of counts charged in the indictment. With Appeals Chamber decisions of the 31st of May, the Trial Chamber accepts the indictment filed on the 21st of January as the operative indictment and will not invite the Prosecution to reduce the indictment further. The Chamber would like, however, to invite the Prosecution to look again at the list of witnesses and the time proposed for examination-in-chief of these witnesses, to see whether it needs, in fact, all these witnesses and all that time. You may or may not want to comment on it right now because, as I said, it's not the business of this Status Conference, but I just wanted to say, can the Prosecution apply its mind to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, the Prosecution will apply its mind to that point. I think we have been fairly conservative, in any event, with the time estimates that we have given, knowing the type of witnesses that we have to call and the evidence that they have to cover. And I think we have really tried to trim it as much as we could in any event. That's my practice, to be as conservative as I can and as cautious as I can. But, Your Honour, I think we could look at it again. There may be some room for a few hours. I can't say anything more than that realistically, knowing the witnesses. And in the case of one or two of them, I may have been overly conservative. So I'm not sure even if I were to give up some, as it were, hours, whether we wouldn't actually lose them again in the modalities of trying to elicit the testimony of particular witnesses involved. Having met with at least two of the most important witnesses it will take a while to get their account out. So with the best will in the world we've tried to be as conservative as we can but as realistic as we can. Of course, I'll look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Rogers. I don't think the Defence would like to comment on this? Okay. I see all of you are shaking your heads indicative of no. The next item would be disclosure. I understand that there are no outstanding issues regarding disclosure pursuant to Rule 66 (A) and (B) and 68 for the time being. Is this understanding correct, Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. For the time being there are no outstanding issues. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you confirm, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct, save in respect obviously of the timetable for trial and the implication of that for disclosure in relation to protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll talk about that. Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to the specific question asked, we concur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As do we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Agreed facts. On the 19th of November, 2010, the parties filed a joint submission on the existence of an armed conflict in Kosovo. Are there any further matters on which the parties have been able to reach agreement, Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: At present, no, Your Honour. There are no further matters upon which we have reached agreement. I don't know whether this is an appropriate moment to pick up this particular point, but, Your Honour, I think for example in relation to the forensics, we may be able to reach some further agreement in relation to that and reduce it down, but in the current form of the -- of what the Defence are prepared to agree as a whole - and not all of them are the same - but what the Defence are able to agree as a whole, we would still have to call some evidence because it doesn't go far enough in the Prosecution's point of view. There may be another way around that, which is most of these witnesses in fact, if not all of them, are down to be 92 bis witnesses and we have a proposal to make, I think, broadly in relation to their -- the acceptance of their evidence as a whole in any event. So it may be that it's not as important as it may at first seem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 92 bis on the question of forensics?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, they're down as 92 bis witnesses, those that cover that area are listed as 92 bis witnesses. So even if we aren't able to reach a form of words that we can all agree, I don't think there is any desire by any of my colleagues to actually re-call these witnesses to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comment, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's been a substantial measure of agreement so far as the forensics is concerned, and indeed the Defence have in effect advanced the same agreed facts in relation to forensics as were advanced and accepted by the Prosecution as sufficient in the original trial. So I hope that any remaining issues in relation to that will be capable of being dealt with very shortly indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. That's more comforting than what I heard from Mr. Rogers on the point. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would concur with what Mr. Emmerson said. With regard to the issue of 92 bis witnesses, I think that raises a different kind of a matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But in terms of forensics, I think it -- we're probably better off than not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I share Mr. Emmerson's optimism, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Prosecution's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the light of the Appeals Chamber's decision, the Prosecution intends to modify its pre-trial brief to reflect the ruling of the Appeals Chamber and to address the issues raised by it. I don't anticipate that the brief will be amended very substantially, and we propose to file an amended brief by the 20th of June, as we discussed yesterday. As I say, it is to address the Appeals Chamber's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May then the Chamber show that -- the record show that the Prosecution is ordered to file its amended pre-trial brief by the 20th of June, 2011. I don't think -- do you want to say anything, Mr. Emmerson, on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Not in relation to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. We will get to the Defence's pre-trial brief. And I don't think Mr. Guy-Smith or Mr. Harvey would like also to comment on this? Thank you so much. Then let's talk about the Defence brief. Is it possible to have this by the 11th of July, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly by the 11th. We, in fact, had offered and suggested the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am aware of that but I was also aware of the fact that Mr. Guy-Smith had indicated yesterday that, as much as he could make it by the 4th, he would prefer the 11th, and I thought it would be well --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate, just in a sentence, foreshadowing issues that are going to follow. We will in the course of our pre-trial brief endeavour to set out such challenges to the admissibility of the evidence on which the Prosecution indicates that it proposes to rely in its amended pre-trial brief as are capable of being identified at the very outset; in other words, the admissibility objections will be identified at the very least, if not fully argued, identified at least in the course of the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's fine, Mr. Emmerson. I'm sitting here trying to imagine how one challenges admissibility without having evidence right here, but you go ahead and write what you have to write and the Chamber will look at it. Mr. Guy-Smith, 11th of July was fine by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, July is fine by me, and with regard to the issue of the admissibility evidence, I probably am going to engage in it the old-fashioned way and deal with it when it arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. You said July, and my specific question --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: July 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Fine by me, of course, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine by you. Thank you so much. Alibi defence or special defence, I'm told that none of the defence teams is proposing to put an alibi or a special defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can confirm that, Your Honour, so far as Mr. Haradinaj is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is certainly not anticipated at this time that such a defence would be mounted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you may be aware from yesterday's hearing record, I did indicate that the Prosecution will not be taken by surprise by Mr. Brahimaj's position that he was for the majority of the indictment period well away from Jabllanice, but he doesn't say that he was never there. That's put in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's quite understandable. Okay, 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater motions. Mr. Rogers, we know that you filed -- you indicated that you intend to call a number of witnesses pursuant to these rules. And I understand that the Prosecution is considering proposing for admission into evidence a large number of transcripts from the original Haradinaj trial and associated exhibits pursuant to 89(F). I also understand that the admission of a large part of these statements is not opposed by the Defence. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what we discussed yesterday. We all recognise we're in a slightly different position in this case, that many of the issues that we wish to litigate have been fully aired in the last trial and there's no need for these witnesses to return for the same issues to be aired. The Court can read the transcripts and look at the associated exhibits and make its conclusion from there. But strictly speaking, a number of those witnesses may not technically fall within 92 bis because they speak to the acts and conduct of the accused. So it's a slightly different position. That's why we've looked at 89(F) as perhaps a way of addressing it between us -- between the parties. A vast majority of the witnesses that we've identified are down as 92 bis witnesses. I think it's about 45 of the total number of witnesses, leaving 10 or 11 as 92 ter or live. What we discussed yesterday was the Defence identifying which of the witnesses on the 92 bis list it was prepared to admit, and that meaning their transcripts and associated trial exhibits that were admitted during the course of the trial would be admitted during the course of these proceedings. We've identified which of those trial exhibits we wish to bring in. If the Defence wish to identify any others from those witnesses, then we can look at that and hopefully try to agree that those come in as well. My learned friend Mr. Guy-Smith indicated yesterday that he thought it would be possible for the Defence to agree the ones he identified as non-contentious 92 bis witnesses by the recess. I was going to respectfully suggest that that could be done in line with the filing of the pre-trial briefs, because I know Mr. Emmerson if he is intending to raise issues of admissibility would already have identified the witnesses from the 92 bis list that he takes issue with plus, I imagine, the parts of their testimony and/or exhibits that he also takes issue with if there are aspects of their testimony that he doesn't like. I would have thought that both my other learned friends could have done the same thing and notify the Prosecution by the 11th of July which witnesses from the 92 bis list it does -- they do not accept should be dealt with in that way, and then we can make such appropriate motions for them and a motion to admit the others, either pursuant by agreement or by -- under 89(F) in the interest of justice in this particular case. That was the way I was thinking that we could deal with the main body of material in this case, leaving the remaining witnesses to be tendered either 92 ter or live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand what you mean by 89(F), in fact. Because I heard you indicate that the witnesses that are 92 bis currently are not necessarily all 92 bis because some of them do refer to the acts and conduct of the accused. And would that -- those category of witnesses not fall under 92 ter and could indeed be part of your motion to say because they are dealing with conduct of the accused, they should be 92 ter and they can come in and be cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the reason we haven't done that is because we don't anticipate anyone wants to cross-examine them --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Further --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- further than they have already been cross-examined. So it's a way of trying to reach by agreement the admission of a body of evidence to best assist the Court and to find a rule that fits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Then I don't understand how -- maybe it's my short understanding, how 92 -- 89(F) is better than 92 bis, but do it the best way you want to do it and we'll look at it when it comes. Mr. Emmerson, you want to make a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply this, so far as the modalities of agreeing the admission of testimony from the previous trial is concerned, I think the parties can discuss that and come up with a joint proposal in respect of those witnesses where there is clear agreement. Subject to one or two observations, if I may. First of all, I think certainly so far as the Defence are concerned, there is unanimity that we would invite the Trial Chamber not to simply work from transcripts but to view the recordings of the testimony of the witness given live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Insofar as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In other words, you are inviting the Chamber to read the transcript of the record of the previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, all of this evidence that we are now referring to is evidence which has been admitted in the original trial, most of it through the giving of oral testimony, either in the form of cross-examination following the admission of a 92 ter statement or because the witness has given evidence live throughout. Now, what is envisaged is that in order to save the re-calling of witnesses in respect of whom the Defence have had a full opportunity to cross-examine the base of the case as it then stood and there are no new issues that need to be traversed, then an appropriate vehicle should be agreed between the parties for putting before the Trial Chamber that witness's evidence as it was placed before the original Trial Chamber. One of the difficulties, and Your Honour will see it in the course of analysing the evidence in due course, is that the Prosecution's pre-trial brief as it stands is taken purely from witness statements without reference to the qualifications, contradictions, and withdrawals that were given in the course of cross-examination. And it will obviously be very important for the Trial Chamber to be very much alive to that in the way that one perhaps could understand the Prosecution hasn't been. And for that purpose, the Defence, as I say, I think speak with one voice that we would not consider it adequate for the Trial Chamber to simply read through the transcripts of those witnesses' evidence. It would be necessary for the Trial Chamber to have available, as did the previous Trial Chamber, such statements as were admitted on the record together with a video-tape of the witness's testimony in order to be in a position to evaluate the witness and the way in which they've given evidence and responded to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then in that event, I think, Mr. Emmerson, it stands to the parties then to put up whatever they want to put up before the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if there's any dissent from that from the Prosecution's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, there's no dissent from that. If my learned friends wish to indicate which of the witnesses they would like the Court to view the videos of, then I -- there's no problem from our point of view in that happening. We're very happy to accommodate, and likewise we may also for some to be viewed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the answer is all witnesses in respect of whom oral testimony was given at the original trial. It's impossible for the re-Trial Chamber to properly evaluate the strength, weight, relevance, demeanour of the witness without seeing them testify and seeing how they respond to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And by oral testimony you included the 92 ter witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Insofar as witnesses were cross-examined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, yeah -- a 92 ter would have been cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean it's plain that the re-Trial Chamber would have available to it the 92 ter witness statement as the original Trial Chamber did. But insofar as the Prosecution wants effectively this Trial Chamber to look at the record of the previous trial, then it must look at the record, not at excerpts from the record or simply the record reduced into written form. So that was the first comment. Secondly, as I think I presaged earlier on, there were some areas of significant difference between the parties as to what should be placed before the re-Trial Chamber. In one respect, there's a witness whom the Defence consider the Prosecution ought to be required to call as a condition of calling another witness in the case in order to ensure that the case is properly and fairly presented. And in a number of instances, there are witnesses that the Prosecution are proposing to call who, notwithstanding and indeed in conformity with the Appeals Chamber's decision, the Defence will submit fall outside the scope of what is properly relevant on the re-trial in the light of the scope of the joint criminal enterprise as it currently stands after the Appeals Chamber decision. In other words, there are still quite a lot of witnesses that the Prosecution wishes to place before the re-Trial Chamber that the Defence disputes the relevance of to the charges on the indictment. And it's in respect of those witnesses, as I presaged a moment ago, that we will identify the position in relation to them in our pre-trial brief. Again, it will be no surprise to anybody because with most of them at least, they were highlighted in the objections raised by way of illustration in the Defence appeal brief which resulted in the present or most recent Appeals Chamber's ruling. But as Your Honour will have seen, the ruling by no means seeks to determine those issues, rather leaving them for the re-Trial Chamber to determine on relevance grounds, and that is a task that in due course will fall to the re-trial Bench. So with those general caveats we are in agreement that an appropriate vehicle would probably be 89(F) by way of agreement in respect of those witnesses where there is agreement, and frankly, the next stage in relation to those where there isn't agreement is for the Trial Chamber to rule on their relevance. Once that ruling has been given, the vehicle by which they are admitted I'm sure is capable of being agreed. In other words, where the Trial Chamber has ruled that notwithstanding Defence objections a particular witness is relevant, it will then be for the Defence to determine whether they want that witness called because we may wish to further cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like you to be quite clear here, Mr. Emmerson. This is a new one on me of -- about a relevant witness. I can understand relevant testimony. Then I've got to hear the testimony to see whether it's relevant or not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, you can -- yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I can't pre-empt a witness from coming to court on the basis that that witness is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour is in a rather different position, in fact, from a position that would pertain in an ordinary trial because you do have the ability to judge precisely that because the only testimony that the Prosecution contends to be relevant is that which was elicited at the original trial. So you're perfectly entitled to view, and indeed that would be the only proper way of determining relevant, to view the testimony that the Prosecution elicited and the Defence elicited from that witness at the original trial, because that's all you're being asked to admit, and then to determine whether that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I will not go into a debate on this one at this point. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution are proposing to call the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's cross that river when we get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, but all I want to flag-up at this stage is that were the Chamber to rule that, for example, witness X was in fact, contrary to Defence submissions, relevant, we would nonetheless reserve the right to require that witness's attendance if it were necessary in due course to put further questions in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then finally, as far as exhibits are concerned, I'm confident that we will be able to provide the Prosecution timeously -- I mean, how quickly I don't want to put a deadline on, but quickly, with the agreed list of exhibits and the further exhibits from the tendered witnesses who are agreed that the Defence wishes to add to the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, that last part, Mr. Emmerson, let me just read it. Okay. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We speak with one voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Amen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not a priest, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Ditto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Rogers, is the Prosecution in a position to file its motions on 92 ter, 92 bis, 92 quater, issues by the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I invited my learned friends to indicate by the 11th of July when they filed their pre-trial briefs which of the witnesses they can agree or not agree pursuant to our I think collective understanding of how best to manage this case. It would be premature for us to do the work to file things under 92 bis, quater, or ter when we're busy trying to agree it by another way, and what I would invite the Court is to allow us -- let me just consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we -- if we have to make 92 ter or quater or the like motions, it will take us a while to put that together. It's not how we have collectively been envisaging managing this. If we have to do that, we think it will take us two weeks to prepare those motions and all the supporting material that's required. I'm hoping that's not necessary. Your Honour, depending upon the date that you set for my learned friends to identify to us which witnesses on our list it's going to agree that we can admit together, from then we would ask 14 days to run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Emmerson said timeously. He didn't say -- and he didn't give us a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, but he was referring to the exhibits not to the witnesses. I've invited the Court to tie that time to the time for the filing of their pre-trial brief, because it seems to me that must be when they know which witnesses they take issue with on the 92 bis list. I think Mr. Emmerson is in agreement with me that that is possible to do. I don't know about my other learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate, in practical terms -- it may be that this just does need a little further explanation. In practical terms, the only issue which is going to divide the parties is relevance. And in so -- I mean, I say that -- I may be contradicted, there may be other side issues, but the central question that will divide the parties is whether the testimony of a particular witness is properly relevant to the issue that this Bench has to try. Insofar as the Defence concedes that a particular witness is relevant, the vehicle for placing that witness's testimony before the re-Trial Chamber is a matter which is capable of agreement between the parties, and subject to there being agreement that the re-Trial Chamber should view the video and not simply read the transcript, then there is unlikely to be any disagreement as regards those witnesses whose relevance is a matter of common ground. But insofar as there are witnesses where the Defence dispute relevance, there is going to need to be a ruling. And we have already indicated in our appeal brief and will indicate with comprehensive clarity in our pre-trial brief who those witnesses are, that is to say which of the witnesses that the Prosecution would currently wish the Trial Chamber to admit the testimony of from the previous trial that the Defence opposes because we say it is not relevant to the issues this re-Trial Chamber now has to try. Once that is clear -- and frankly, it is clear already because the Prosecution knows exactly who we're talking about because we identified them in our appeal brief so they can get on with their work already, but we will formally put our position again on the record in the pre-trial brief, which is why I foreshadowed that when I was referring to the pre-trial brief. And from that point onwards, it will be necessary for the Prosecution to persuade the Trial Chamber that the material ought to be admitted and the form in which it ought to be admitted. And I'm simply saying, as I said earlier on, we reserve the right to seek to cross-examine those witnesses and we make no concessions, and the Prosecution should not expect that we will, on the manner in which the form in which or the rubric under the rules through which their evidence may come to be admitted. We maintain a solid objection in respect of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And on the assumption it's ditto, amen, can I say now I understand you better. I would still want to see if I can't get all this within the date of the 27th of June. You've just said, Mr. Emmerson, that the Prosecution is aware of who are those witnesses that you object to. Is it not possible therefore - now purely from a practical point of view - for the parties to agree the 92 bis witnesses that they agree on who are -- you've -- all parties feel are relevant and using 89(F) file those and that's over, there's no need for a 92 bis motion about them any longer. Then the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- file a motion with respect to those witnesses that relevance is challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And let the Chamber decide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And let -- I would like to be able to -- I'm trying to find out whether that agreement can't be reached much earlier than the 27th of June to enable the Prosecution to have the two weeks they need to mount a motion with respect to those that the Defence challenges the relevance of.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I respond to that? First of all, as I think Your Honour is aware, we would not stand in the way of any measure which would speed these proceedings up. So although this is a change of timetable that Your Honour is proposing from the one that naturally follows from the timetables so far suggested, I see no reason in principle. And on this I may not -- it may be a situation in which the Defence does not speak with one voice, but on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj at least, I can say we would certainly be in a position to advance the timetable in that way. The Prosecution meanwhile can be getting on with drafting their applications in respect of those witnesses the relevance of which they are very well aware that the Defence dispute and they can use our appeal brief as their guide for that. In the meantime, before the 27th, we would be in a position to indicate so far as the Defence are concerned which of those witnesses whose testimony the Prosecution does propose to adduce there is not going to be any dispute about. Your Honour, in short, anything which shortens the timetable in that way we are more than prepared to accommodate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, it was not my intention to take the same method in the pre-trial brief for the Balaj Defence as was foreshadowed by Mr. Emmerson. I believe that with regard to some of the witnesses that can be agreed, we may be able to meet the 27th date. I'm not confident that we will be able to do that with all of them, but I think we can reach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me be clear you understand the request from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The request is not to meet the 27th June date by way of agreement. It is to reach agreement early enough to enable the Prosecution to make the 27th June date with its motion on the witnesses that are disagreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may correct my English there. On the witnesses about whom there is disagreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that that could possibly constitute a problem because -- and I -- having just clearly understood what Your Honour has said and knowing the way that we have worked before and I think we have worked efficiently before inter-party, that is a very short period of time, I think, to deal with all of the issues, although some of these witnesses have already been identified and the Prosecution has some guidance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I for the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say it takes long because they have already been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's some of them. There are a series of other witnesses that don't fall into that category. And in the absence of an understanding with regard to when we are going to be receiving disclosure for those witnesses that we have heretofore not received disclosure and to the extent that those witnesses' testimony will impact upon some of these pre-existing witnesses, I think I would be remiss in making a commitment in terms of definiteness with regard to what I can agree to because I don't have the entire picture in hand. If I had all of the disclosure, I would be much more sanguine to be able to say to the Court that we would be in a position to give a more robust and quicker response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just noticed, working backwards, that would require agreement between the parties or at least an indication of agreement between the parties tomorrow -- or Friday at the latest, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tomorrow is Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, Your Honour's quite right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hold it there. Let's hear Mr. Harvey and then I'll ask a question. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in the same situation as my friends for the Defence here. My client's position is he wants to move this re-trial forward as fast as possible and wants me to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I appreciate that he wants me to do nothing to slow down that process. We will work and hard and fast as we can but there are certain things which simply cannot be accomplished by tomorrow, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I see your client is nodding in agreement with you at back there. Okay. Then my question is, I'm throwing myself into the hands of the parties, give me a suggested date. You gave a suggested date earlier, Mr. Rogers, I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did only because that was the pre-trial brief date of the 11th of July. Your Honour, the Prosecution awaits the identification of the witness. As soon as we have it, we do our 14 days and move it on. I'm confident that my learned friends, and certainly Mr. Emmerson appears to be in a position to move forward, know who are the contested witnesses. They have all been in a trial that I wasn't involved in. They should know of the 92 bis witnesses which ones they take issue with and they can identify that very quickly, I would have thought. It's a matter for Your Honour. As long as I have 14 days from then, we can get on with it. And I would like to say we have done a fair amount of the work already. It's not that we have been sitting idly by, it's just that we need to finish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Now when you talking about "as long as I can have 14 days from then." This date of the 11th of July, what are you asking for? For them to submit to you what they object to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. I only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you need 14 days after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thereafter, yes. If Your Honour brings the date of the 11th forward, I just need 14 days from then, So it doesn't matter to me when it is. The only reason I suggested that was because that was the date for the pre-trial brief and it had some logical consistency that all of that came together with the pre-trial brief identifying the admissibility issues together with the witnesses that they took issue with. But if Your Honour brings that forward, I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that logical consistency?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, it makes -- it's logically internally consistent. There are really two stages to this. The first is for the Prosecution to be told which witnesses are agreed and which are contested on relevance grounds. We can do that within seven days of today. The Prosecution would thereafter request 14 days to file motions in respect of those who are not agreed. And the second stage is the 11th, which would be the date from which we would outline the basis for our objection, but the Prosecution don't need to know that in detail, although they already do know it because it's outlined in the appeal brief, but they don't need formal notification of it because all they need to know at the moment is who do they not need to make an application for. And we can give that indication for certain within seven days. So that will bring the Prosecution's timetable forward, if we say seven days from today is the 17th, to the 5th of August, which would be the day after the filing of their -- I'm sorry, the 5th of July -- no it wouldn't be the 5th of July. I turned over two pages. It would be the 1st, I think, is that right? The 1st of July, which would be the Friday before they're due to -- am I right? Do we have a 4th of July dead-line for the Prosecution? No. Very well. So the 1st of July, that would give them until the 1st of July to file the motions that Your Honour has in mind, so that's a few days longer than Your Honour originally envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the one-liner answer is you can give this answer within seven days?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the Balaj Defence be able to do that in seven days?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's -- well, anything's possible, which is why I'm saying we'll do our best, Your Honour. I mean, I understand -- I understand what the Court wants, and I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court is prepared to accommodate you if you are not able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I keep on -- and I know I'm kind of beating the same horse that I've always beaten, which is if I have the entirety of the disclosure so I know the entire case that I'm facing, then I'm in a position to deal with the entire case. But in the absence of that, I'm in a position where, as logical as this may seem in the abstract, I feel as if I'm putting the cart before the horse because there's information that I do not have. There is disclosure that I do not have available to me. If I have that disclosure available, for example, if the disclosure which we have discussed on a number of occasions, the subject of protective measures, was made available to me tomorrow, then I would be in a position to meet this particular dead-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The short answer is you're not able to meet that dead-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I make a practical suggestion. I know I've been jumping up and down on my feet. What would normally happen in a situation like this if the parties are not in a position to agree, they simply object, which may result in overbroad objections. May I suggest that the Defence give within whatever time-frame the Trial Chamber sets an indication of its understanding of its present position, but if obviously that were to be modified as a result of disclosure, then any formal consent would not have been provided for the evidence to be admitted and the matter can be reconsidered in the light of any disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Thank you. I see, Mr. Guy-Smith, you are trying to stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You made a comment with regard to what Mr. Emmerson said and I was waiting for that to come up. I thought I heard you say "it's all right," but I'm not sure that's what I did hear you say or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't appear on the screen but I think that's what I said, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To that effect. With that in mind, then I'm in a different position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then I understand you. Mr. Harvey, you do not want to delay the trial of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You got that right. Now, I think we can go along to -- with what Mr. Emmerson has just suggested. I think in reality as far as my client's position is concerned, the bulk of this is going to be covered by what Mr. Emmerson has already said was in his appeal brief and will be part of the position he takes. I don't think we are likely to be having any very different position from that. If that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can I summarise the situation by saying that within seven days from today, the Defence, to the extent possible, will give to the Prosecution the list of names of those 92 bis witnesses whose relevance they object to to enable the Prosecution to file its motion with respect to such witnesses by no later than the 27th of June, with the caveat that as disclosure takes place and there are further witnesses to whom or against whom the Defence objects, of course the Defence will always have the right to object. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That caveat is trying to cover you, Mr. Guy-Smith, and I'm trying to look at you to see whether I can get a nod from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that okay with you, Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my calculation is if they have a week from today, that's the 16th of June, which takes us to the 30th of June, which was the 30 days -- the 14 days that I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 30th June, I can give you to the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll do obviously whatever the Court asks us to do. It's unfortunate that we may not be getting the final position which requires us to waste time making applications which are actually unnecessary because the Defence collectively is not in a position to indicate which witnesses it thinks it can and cannot agree. Mr. Emmerson has made very clear that he can do that. I'm at a loss to understand why my learned friends for the other two accused cannot also do that, but they say they can't, and unless Your Honour makes a firm order and we -- then we have to live with what comes in seven days' time and take it from there. But we'll do whatever Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you made a comment which I feel I've got to respond to. "It's unfortunate that we may not be getting the final decision which requires us to waste time making applications which are actually unnecessary ..." Now, I don't want unnecessary applications. Do you want to go back to your original suggestion that we give you up to the 11th of July to sort yourselves out and would you then tell us that by the 11th of July you would have a final decision amongst yourselves as to who is objected against and who is not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in my learned friends' hands. The concerns are being expressed by them as to when they feel they can tell us who they do and do not object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but Mr. Rogers, I'm sorry, I must cut you short here. You can't have your cake and eat it. You made the suggestion which I've tried not to agree with and I'm trying to go back to your own suggestion. Now, you cannot now say you are in your learned friends' hands. If I give you up to the 11th and then give you another two weeks after that, I want a firm commitment from you that you are going to live by those dead-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me. I suggested the 11th of July to assist my learned friends in identifying the witnesses that they want to object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I have been able to live with any date that the Court sets for me to make applications. I've asked for 14 days for me when they tell me who they object to. That's how all of this started and now I feel that the Prosecution comes and looks as though it's trying to move goal-posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm not suggesting you've been moving goal-posts. What I'm saying -- look --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If you give me until the 11th of July that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson says he can give you in seven days the witnesses he objects to. Mr. Guy-Smith says he can give you in seven days the witnesses he objects to once he has got full disclosure. Now, there is no full disclosure right now. Okay. There isn't going to be full disclosure in the next seven days, so we've got to live with the fact that Mr. Guy-Smith is not going to be able to give you his final word on this issue until he has received full disclosure, whenever that takes place. Mr. Harvey is very much in line with Mr. Emmerson's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, neither of whom seem to have difficulties with the disclosure problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Because it seems to us, respectfully, that the disclosure that will be coming does not touch any of these particular witnesses under 92 bis. But in any event, I will abide with such orders as Your Honour considers appropriate for the effective management of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that Mr. Rogers may wish to try the case for me but I respectfully decline. And whether or not he understands what my concerns are or not is more the pity for him, not for my client. However, we have spent quite a bit of time together. I have been in this Tribunal for quite a bit of time, and I believe that I can stand firm with the proposition that I do not waste time, I do not intend on wasting time, and I look for clarity and quick solutions to many things whenever they can be achieved. An easy way of settling this whole matter would be if Mr. Rogers would give us disclosure now, which is something I have repeatedly suggested to him and he repeatedly declines because he believes that he is in a position to stand by the Court's previous decision and he does not choose to give us disclosure prior to that time. I can't do much about that. I'm trying to figure out a way of effectively and efficiently dealing with this case. The way that one effectively and efficiently deals with a case is they are given the entirety of the information that is in the possession of their opponent here, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I'm now going to make a ruling. Today is the 9th. By the 16th of June, the Defence must file -- or by no later than that date, the Defence must file and give to the Prosecution the list of witnesses that they object to to enable the Prosecution to file its motion pursuant to Rules 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater by no later than the 27th of June, this year. That's the ruling and that disposes of that item. Now, the next item I would like us to talk about is the sitting schedule. The Chamber has indicated earlier that it won't be able to sit on a five-day-per-week schedule as two of the members of the Bench appointed for the pre-trial are also sitting in another case. The Chamber has informed the parties of the issue via the Chamber's Legal Officer and had inquired about the parties' preferences regarding the available scheduling options. The Chamber has also sought that the use of other sections of the Tribunal, the Registry in particular. The Prosecution has indicated it would prefer a two-week block sitting on a five-day-per-week basis. Counsel for Balaj and Brahimaj have indicated that they will need to raise the matter further with OLAD. Counsel for Haradinaj has indicated that he would prefer block sitting on a one-week basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One or two. Thanks. Thank you. Is there anything further from the parties? Have you heard from OLAD, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have not heard from OLAD. I have no idea what their position is. If I was dealing with the matter of trial efficiency and only that matter, I would suggest two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I'm dealing with the ability to defend my client because I will be able to resource a team, I have no idea because I don't know what OLAD's position is with regard to that issue. I'm trying to work that out. Hopefully I will be able to. If I cannot, I will make the appropriate report to the Chamber and I will take appropriate measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I second what Mr. Guy-Smith has said. I think Your Honour is also aware that I have an additional complication, that I am lead counsel on the stand-by team in the Karadzic case which sits in the mornings. Now, it we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Welcome to the party. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And I know you've got your problems. I know all of the Judges involved here have got serious conflict problems, and I do understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I would be most grateful if you would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, you also said you wanted a two-week block. Okay. Fine. It looks like -- let me just give an indication before we get to that point just to close this point, that it looks like we will go for the two-week block then. Is there any other business that the parties would like to raise at this point? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the elephant in the room. I was hoping that Your Honour might indicate when the hearing date may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Whether it's going to be anticipated before the recess or after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can raise that, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I will -- please do remind me to come back to this item at the end, then. With respect to the start of the trial, if there are no further matters that need to be resolved at this stage, the Trial Chamber would propose to hold a Pre-Trial Conference on Wednesday, the 17th of August, and to hear opening statements on the 18th of August. The presentation of evidence can then begin immediately thereafter, and the Chamber would be sitting on the 17th, 18th, and 19th of August for that entire week and also -- and for the entire week starting the 22nd of August, following which it will break for two weeks to enable the Stanisic and the Zupljanin trial to sit for two full weeks. So briefly speaking, we would sit 17th, 18th, 19th, and then we would sit the week of the 22nd of August. And from then on would start sitting on the 12th of September, the week of the 12th of September, and the week of the 19th of September, 10th of October, on and on and on. Okay. How does that sound?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two comments, if I may. First of all, we would on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj strongly prefer at least the formal opening of the trial before the recess, even if shortly before the recess. There are a number of reasons for that, one of them of course is the simple reason that we have clients who have been in pre-trial custody, and certainly in my client's case following a complete acquittal, for a year, and the sooner the trial starts the better. Another is that the timetable for disclosure in respect of protected witnesses, and one in particular, back-dates from the trial date. And we're obviously extremely anxious to be in a position to investigate -- I don't want to -- I don't want to depart from the formality of the proceedings, but the reality is that both parties know this is a two-witness trial. And one of those -- I mean there are two central --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Water under the bridge, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, no, it isn't. I mean in the sense that we both know, both sides of the courtroom know that there are two key witnesses in this case and one of them we are simply not in a position to investigate and that is the one under the pseudonym 81. And the sooner we are in a position to start that investigation, the sooner we are going to be in a position to know how long the investigation is going to take and what material we may need to place before the Trial Chamber. If the trial date start goes back until the rear part of August, that means in practical terms we're not going to get disclosure until the second half of next month, just as the Court is moving into recess time, which means that the recess period, obviously people have planned the recess period in advance because nobody understood or expected the trial to be in the position it is time-wise now, would be the period during which one would expect operative investigations to take place. So unless the Prosecution is in the position -- and I understand Mr. Rogers is entitled to stand on his rights within the rulings as they are, but unless the Prosecution is in a position to waive by way of truncating the time-frame for disclosure, as Mr. Guy-Smith suggested a moment ago, and to give disclosure sooner, then the effect of ordering the start date of the trial to go back into the second half of August is in effect to undermine the period for investigation the Defence have available in respect of that witness. And so we would strongly urge the Trial Chamber to consider for at least the formal opening of the trial in the week before the July recess. That's the first thing. The second thing is very much a personal concern, and that -- all parties have been discussing what the trial schedule was going to look like, in other words, whether it was going to be one week on/one week off, two weeks on/two weeks off, or part week and part week, and none of us had any idea of the start date for the trial. But I have indicated in the past to the Registry that I have difficulties with two dates in September, both of which I have long pre-existing prior commitments in the European Court of Human Rights in interstate litigation, which fall now within the two-week slab that Your Honour has indicated that this trial will be sitting. I am simply not in a position to change those commitments. They existed long before this re-trial was set and of course at the time when no one anticipated that the Appeals Chamber's would take six months to deliver their judgement in relation to this matter. And that being the case, we're going to need, I'm afraid, to find some process for navigating how we structure the time during September because on the timetable that Your Honour has just set, and anticipating what Mr. Rogers has indicated already about how long the witnesses are likely to take and the order in which he wishes to call them, the timetable that Your Honour has just said would put key witnesses on days when I simply cannot be here. And I think, if I may say so, we're all in a very difficult situation managing this trial because of what has happened managerially within this Tribunal over the last six months, and we need to find some way of bringing matters forward so the trial can be conducted efficiently and everybody can be represented appropriately by their counsel who have represented them throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me start with your last point. Your last point, I think, is -- is irrelevant to the point at issue and it can always be discussed and accommodated at the time it arises. You have given notice of it now, at least to me, and the Chamber may be apprised of it, that you might be indisposed for some time in September. And I don't think that you're dealing here with unreasonable people.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: People who would be prepared to accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's two days only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. That's fine. But that has nothing to do, in my understanding, with whether we start before or after recess. Let me address your first point now. Your first point, as I understand it, is doing exactly what -- is undermining the decision of this Chamber previously on the question of disclosure. The question of disclosure -- a decision has been rendered where the Chamber said it will be either 30 days before the trial or 45 days before the witness is called or whichever or whatever way, 45 days before the trial -- I can't remember, but there is that decision. And if we start before recess, you're getting on top of that period three more weeks. And as you rightly said, it is within Mr. Rogers to decide whether or not he wants to truncate that time or he wants to stick by his rights. As things stand now, the Chamber has granted him those rights and either -- either the Chamber is going to undo that because of a motion that comes from either of the parties or Mr. Rogers decides --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- as the person benefitting from that decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I add to Your Honour's point because in fact that may seem to be position but it isn't. The order in fact -- and the devil is in the detail. The order is that the disclosure should be given 45 days before the witness testifies or 30 days before the start of the trial, whichever is the earlier. Now, if Your Honour were to fix the start of the trial for, let us say, the week before the recess, then back-dating it 30 days would take us to some time fairly soon, I think the end of next week. But the Defence would have been entitled to the disclosure 45 days as a minimum before the witness testifies, which would take us pretty much to the end of the recess. In other words, had the Prosecution given disclosure 30 days before trial due to start immediately before the recess, they still wouldn't have been able to call the witness until after the recess because the way that the order is framed gives the Defence the benefit of the longest period. So in fact, the point that Your Honour makes is apparent but not real.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do not -- I do not have a copy of that decision before me and I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can read Your Honour the operative paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be that as it may -- or even before I respond, I thought I saw Mr. Rogers wanting to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to say that even with the -- if we were to start on the 18th of August, 45 days would take us, I think, to the 4th of July, so my learned friends would obtain the materials if we were anticipating on calling the witness very shortly thereafter, to, you know, boxing and coxing a day or two, would be receiving disclosure around about the 4th of July in any event. So I'm not sure that the point my learned friend makes is good in the particular circumstances of this case, because we end up in more or less the same type of position. It's 45 days before the start -- 45 days before the testimony of the witness and if we anticipated this witness would be one of the first witnesses, then the disclosure would be coming a bit earlier. But in any event, Your Honour, we support the position that Your Honour has taken in relation to the days and for the -- and the reasons why the decision was originally given. And we also considered that the 17th -- that week of the 17th/18th of August gives us a good date to work to to issue such summonses and subpoenas as we may require to enable the start of the trial to be as clean as it possibly can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just respond to that last point, because if Mr. Rogers is prepared to work on that hypothesis, the one he's just advanced upon the record to Your Honour, the start date is the 18th July. Working back 45 days he is required to give disclosure on the 4th of July. Can I ask him to confirm that that is exactly what the Prosecution intends to do because that may resolve some of the problems. If he's prepared to commit himself now to treating the start date of the trial as the date effective for the 45 days and to give disclosure on the 4th of July, that would certainly assist in resolving some of these difficulties. Can I ask him indicate his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Swift off his feet as ever, Mr. Emmerson seeks to seek an advantage. I understand quite properly why he does that. Your Honour, as I've said before, we will give the disclosure in the time-frame that has been permitted by the Court. If we were to call him on the 22nd of August, then we would be giving disclosure six weeks beforehand. He's not going to be coming on the 18th. If he's coming at all, it could be in the following week. So my learned friends will receive the information in -- with good time, with six weeks for them to be able to investigate before the witness comes, which is all they're entitled to. They may have had a shorter period of time if the witness was coming on day one, but because of the particular recess I -- what I was trying to say is they are really getting to what they're entitled to anyway if Your Honour takes this start date. I don't think it makes a lot of difference if it was immediately before in terms of this additional time for investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that detail you can sort out between yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I didn't mean to take an unfair advantage. Mr. Rogers made a submission to Your Honour that it made no difference to disclosure because we were going to get it anyway on the 4th of July because that's when he was going to be planning to call the witness. Now, if the position is that that is not the case, then he shouldn't have made that submission to Your Honour. If the position is that that is the case, then he should say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: By way of illustration and sometimes I try to be helpful and I wish I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You wish you hadn't ? Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sometimes. You are bound anyway by that decision, to give them either 45 days or 30 days before a certain event takes place, and you will do so, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. In that event then -- yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the risk of stating the obvious, I know this is an order and a decision that has been made by this Court. It was made at a different time in a different context and with different contemplation of where we would all be by this date, in fact probably in contemplation that this trial would have been finished by this date. At the point that we find ourselves in now, it is in my view appropriate, and I -- you may well wish and prefer this to be done on papers, but it is in my view appropriate for the Court to entertain reconsideration of that order in order to give the Defence what it truly needs in a timely fashion because in a timely fashion is not something that happens just a couple of days before the recess. If we could have that information now, it would make everybody's lives so much simpler. And I, for the life of me, cannot see -- I can see why a Prosecutor would sit on something because I've got an order from the Court. Unless the Court tells me, I don't have to do anything different from what I've got, and if all it is going to take to shift this blockage that we all are facing at the moment is for the Court to reconsider its order, then I would strongly urge and invite the Court to do so. Whether you would wish me to do that orally or in writing I think it is appropriate for reconsideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know how -- I don't know how -- whether you do want to put it on paper or you feel you have made your submissions fully now, Mr. Harvey. Let me say, yes, it is true from what you say that this decision was taken at a different time under different circumstances. We didn't know where we would be. Maybe you are right. I'm not quite sure how far right you are that we probably might have finished this case by today. However, you are not right when you say the Prosecutor is sitting on the order simply because he's got an order. He's sitting on the order simply because of the underlying reasons for that order, the underlying reasons for that order was protective measures for certain witnesses and those protective measures were given for specific reasons and those times were put there for specific reasons. Okay. Those -- unless you say the reasons for giving that order have changed, I do not see how you can ask for a review of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'll take that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just not an order for the sake of an order that he's sitting on it. It's because of the underlying reasons for that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I don't think I'm going to take it further here on my feet, but I will think further about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Think further about it, Mr. Harvey. Thank you so much. Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate what the Court said. I'm pleased to know that Mr. Rogers at times wishes to be helpful and suggested July 4th as the date to be helpful to the Defence. With regard to the discussion that was just had, one of the difficulties that exists, Your Honour, is that with regard to the information that the Court looked at in terms of making this order, we were uninformed. We requested that the ex parte submissions that were made to the Court be made available to the Defence so that we were in a position to respond intelligently and meaningfully to those submissions. However, such is not the case. So once again we remain -- and I have full confidence that based upon the information the Court had at the time, in the absence of any comment or submission made by the Defence, that the decision and the order made is one that is reasoned and logical. However, we still remain in the same position because one of the issues that -- and I think the Court is appreciative of this. One of the issues that is really hotly contested with regard to this particular case is the extent to which that particular drum, the drum of intimidation or the drum of fear, is beaten. But we're not in a position to intelligently respond to that because we don't know what the submissions were, and I leave it at that. I leave it at that because I'm not going to ask you to reconsider an order for any reason at this point in time, and what I really was hoping to do and what I've been attempting to do literally for months is see whether or not Mr. Rogers would be in a position to see his way clear to allowing for this matter to proceed efficiently with full disclosure so that we can get to the point that we all want to get to, which is to try this case and deal with the substantive issues that rightfully belong before Your Honour and the Chamber that ultimately sits on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you for saying you will not take it any further than that because, in fact, if you were then given the material that the Chamber is privy to when it made this decision, then this discussion would not be there, disclosure would have been made anyway and there are certain -- this delayed disclosure --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm ignorant of what you were supplied with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course you are ignorant of what I was supplied with and that is precisely the issue. The issue is that we're being requested to keep you ignorant until 45 days before start of trial. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I hate being ignorant, I think you can appreciate that. And the sooner that I'm educated, the happier I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's no shame to be ignorant. It might be a shame just not to understand things, but it is no shame to be ignorant. I might not know what is behind this thing, it doesn't make -- it's no shame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we understand each other well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. In that event, is there any other submissions? In that event, we will start on the 17th of August, as explained earlier. May I now go back to the item of other business. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I simply thank Your Honour for the indication that flexibility will be shown in respect of my difficulties in September and can I formally place on the record the two dates concerned, they are the 14th and the 22nd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are not even consecutive?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, they are separate dates, separated by nearly a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that advanced notice, Mr. Emmerson, and we'll look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do remind us at the appropriate times timeously. Don't rely on me remembering --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I shall and I will keep in close touch with Mr. Rogers as well, and I'm sure he understands that he will need to schedule his case around those dates. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Anything, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. In that event, Mr. Haradinaj, is there anything you would like to raise regarding your health or conditions of detention?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Haradinaj. Mr. Balaj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BALAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Everything is fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Brahimaj. I think, then, there being nothing else to do, I can safely say we stand adjourned and we will see each other on the 17th of August. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.20 p.m.
